rules.relevance: The proviso states that where a transfer is chargeable to gift tax or exempt under Section 5 of the Gift Tax Act 'for any assessment year commencing after the 31st day of March, 1964', the value of such assets shall not be included in computing net wealth. The interpretation of this phrase is the core of the dispute.

rules.case_name: State of Punjab vs Prem Sukhdas
rules.reference: State of Punjab vs Prem Sukhdas
rules.relevance: Cited to establish that the rule of preferring a constitutional construction cannot be used to alter the clear meaning of statutory words or repeal statutory provisions.

rules.case_name: Ahmed G.H. Ariff and Others vs Commissioner of Wealth tax, Calcutta
rules.reference: Ahmed G.H. Ariff and Others vs Commissioner of Wealth tax, Calcutta
rules.relevance: Held that 'annuity' in the Wealth Tax Act must be given its legal signification, requiring a fixed sum payable yearly.

rules.reference: Uttar Pradesh Krishi Utpadhan Mandi Adhiniyam, 1964
rules.relevance: Empowers the State Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the Act.

rules.reference: Bombay Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1939
rules.relevance: These sections define the procedure for declaring market areas, establishing market committees, and establishing markets, which is central to the validity of the committee's powers.

rules.reference: Rules framed under the Bombay Agricultural Produce Markets Act
rules.relevance: The court struck down these rules as ultra vires because they authorized the Market Committee to issue licenses for the entire market area, encroaching on the Commissioner's power under Section 4(2) proviso before a market was established.

rules.reference: Rules framed under the Bombay Agricultural Produce Markets Act
rules.relevance: The court held this rule ultra vires because it allowed fee fixation without the State Government prescribing maxima as required by Section 11.

rules.case_name: M. C. V. Arunachala Nadar vs The State of Madras
rules.reference: M. C. V. Arunachala Nadar vs The State of Madras
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to uphold the constitutionality of regulating agricultural produce markets, finding no material difference between the Madras Act and the Bombay Act.

rules.case_name: Syed Mohamed & Company vs State of Andhra
rules.reference: Syed Mohamed & Company vs State of Andhra
rules.relevance: Cited to support the view that Rule 16(5) was not ultra vires the rule-making authority.

rules.reference: Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939
rules.relevance: Defined 'sale' for pre-Constitution period based on territorial nexus (presence of goods or production in Province).

rules.reference: Madras General Sales Tax (Turnover and Assessment) Rules, 1939
rules.relevance: Provided that sales by unlicensed dealers are liable to taxation on each occasion, which the court held was not ultra vires.

rules.case_name: V. M. Syed Mohammed & Co. vs The State of Madras
rules.reference: V. M. Syed Mohammed & Co. vs The State of Madras
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case, noting that the finding of Rule 16(5) being ultra vires was not necessary for the decision as the parties were licensed dealers.

rules.case_name: State of Jammu & Kashmir vs Caltex (India) Ltd.
rules.reference: State of Jammu & Kashmir vs Caltex (India) Ltd.
rules.relevance: Held that a single assessment order can be split up and dissected if items of sale can be separated and taxed for different periods.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Defines 'wife' to include a woman who has been divorced by or has obtained a divorce from her husband and has not remarried, forming the basis of the appellant's claim.

rules.provision: Explanation to the second proviso to Section 125(3)
rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Defines 'just ground' for a wife's refusal to live with her husband, specifically stating that if a husband contracts marriage with another woman or keeps a mistress, it shall be considered a just ground.

rules.case_name: Chand Begum vs Hyderbaig
rules.reference: Chand Begum vs Hyderbaig
rules.relevance: Held that a husband who marries again cannot compel the first wife to share the conjugal home with a co-wife, and an offer to maintain her on such condition is not bona fide.

rules.case_name: Mohd. A. Khan vs Shah Bano Begum
rules.reference: Mohd. A. Khan vs Shah Bano Begum
rules.relevance: Established that Section 125 overrides personal law and that the Explanation confers the right to refuse to live with a husband who contracts another marriage.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
rules.relevance: Distinguishes between divorce by the husband and divorce obtained by the wife, supporting the interpretation that the legislature contemplated both modes under Section 125.

rules.case_name: The State of Andhra vs Sri Arisetty Sriramulu
rules.reference: The State of Andhra vs Sri Arisetty Sriramulu
rules.relevance: The Full Bench in this case held that 'facts' includes evidentiary facts even if intentionally withheld. The Supreme Court distinguished this view, holding that such an interpretation puts a premium on fraud and negligence.

rules.reference: Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957
rules.relevance: This provision grants exemption from sales tax for goods specified in the Fourth Schedule. The court interpreted Entry 7 to determine if tobacco seed oil and cake are exempt.

rules.case_name: Dilworth vs Commissioners of Stamps
rules.reference: Dilworth vs Commissioners of Stamps
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to establish that the joint use of 'mean' and 'include' in a definition clause renders the definition exhaustive.

rules.case_name: State of Andhra Pradesh vs Abdul Bakshi & Bros.
rules.reference: State of Andhra Pradesh vs Abdul Bakshi & Bros.
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case because the goods in question (tanning bark) were consumed in manufacturing, whereas the arc furnaces were fixed assets not consumed or converted.

rules.reference: Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939
rules.relevance: The provision allows the Appellate Tribunal to review an order on the basis of 'facts which were not before it when it passed the order'. The court had to determine if this phrase covers facts withheld due to deliberate negligence.

rules.case_name: Tata Oil Mill Co. Ltd. v. Workmen
rules.reference: Tata Oil Mill Co. Ltd. v. Workmen
rules.relevance: Confirmed that if an order of discharge is punitive, mala fide, or amounts to victimisation, the Industrial Court can set it aside.

rules.reference: Tribunal's Power to Adjudicate on Merits without Enquiry
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that if no domestic enquiry is held, the Tribunal can still uphold termination if the employer proves misconduct on merits with satisfactory evidence.

rules.case_name: Management of U. B. Dutt & Co. v. Workmen of U. B. Dutt & Co.
rules.reference: Management of U. B. Dutt & Co. v. Workmen of U. B. Dutt & Co.
rules.relevance: Distinguished on facts; that case involved a colourable exercise of power to avoid a departmental enquiry for misconduct, whereas the present case involved bona fide loss of confidence.

rules.case_name: Punjab National Bank Ltd. vs Its Workmen
rules.reference: Punjab National Bank Ltd. vs Its Workmen
rules.relevance: Cited to establish that even if a domestic enquiry is not held or is invalid, the employer can justify termination on merits before the Tribunal by producing satisfactory evidence of misconduct.

rules.case_name: Workmen of Motipur Sugar Factory (P) Ltd. vs Motipur Sugar Factory
rules.reference: Workmen of Motipur Sugar Factory (P) Ltd. vs Motipur Sugar Factory
rules.relevance: Relied on for the principle that if a domestic enquiry is irregular or not held, the Tribunal can adjudicate on the merits and justify discharge if misconduct is proved.

rules.reference: Income Tax Act, 1961
rules.relevance: Prescribes interest rates on refunds. The court held it was not directly applicable to the LIC's liability for delayed payment of policy proceeds, rejecting the argument that the 15% rate was excessive.

rules.reference: Income Tax Act, 1961
rules.relevance: Empowers the ITO to require a person holding money for an assessee to pay that money to the ITO to satisfy tax arrears.

rules.reference: Income Tax Act, 1961
rules.relevance: Provides the mechanism for a person receiving a notice to object by filing a statement on oath that the sum is not due to the assessee. The court held this is a statutory obligation that must be performed promptly to discharge liability.

rules.reference: Income Tax Act, 1961
rules.relevance: Deems a person who fails to make payment in pursuance of a notice as an assessee in default. The court used this to show the real risk to the LIC was in failing to object properly, rather than in making a true statement.

rules.reference: Necessary party in writ proceedings
rules.relevance: The court held that the ITO was not a necessary party because the relief sought was solely against the LIC for interest, and no relief was claimed against the ITO.

rules.case_name: N. P. Ponnuswami vs Returning Officer, Namakkal Constituency
rules.reference: N. P. Ponnuswami vs Returning Officer, Namakkal Constituency
rules.relevance: Defines 'election' as the entire process culminating in the declaration of a candidate elected, supporting the view that the voter list must remain constant throughout.

rules.reference: Mysore Municipalities (Election of Councillors) Rules, 1965
rules.relevance: Confers power of superintendence, direction, and control on the State Government to ensure elections are held in accordance with the Act; the central issue was whether this power allowed cancelling the election calendar.

rules.reference: Karnataka Municipalities Act, 1964
rules.relevance: Establishes that the list of voters is conclusive evidence for determining qualification to vote or be elected, implying a single list for the entire election process.

rules.reference: Karnataka Municipalities Act, 1964
rules.relevance: Deems the Electoral Roll of the Legislative Assembly for the area included in a division to be the list of voters for that division.

rules.case_name: Shivappa Chanamollappa Jogendra vs Basavannappa Gadlappa Banker
rules.reference: Shivappa Chanamollappa Jogendra vs Basavannappa Gadlappa Banker
rules.relevance: Supports the view that the relevant Electoral Roll is the one in force when the election process commences.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Income Tax v. Abdullabhai Abdulkadar
rules.reference: Commissioner of Income Tax v. Abdullabhai Abdulkadar
rules.relevance: Approved the definition of a business debt as one that springs directly from carrying on business and is incidental to it.

rules.case_name: Curtis v. L. & G. Oldfield Ltd.
rules.reference: Curtis v. L. & G. Oldfield Ltd.
rules.relevance: Established that a 'bad debt' must be a trading debt that would have swelled profits if recovered, distinguishing it from a mere advance.

rules.reference: Income Tax Act, 1922
rules.relevance: Allows deduction for expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for business purposes, excluding capital expenditure and personal expenses.

rules.case_name: Arunachalam Chettiar v. Commissioner of Income Tax
rules.reference: Arunachalam Chettiar v. Commissioner of Income Tax
rules.relevance: Reinforced the principle that a bad debt must be one that, if good, would have come in to swell taxable profits.

rules.reference: Nature of Transaction vs. Memorandum of Association
rules.relevance: The real nature of a transaction is deduced from the circumstances in which it took place, not merely from the objects clause in the Memorandum of Association.

rules.case_name: Binod Singh vs District Magistrate, Dhanbad, Bihar and Ors.
rules.reference: Binod Singh vs District Magistrate, Dhanbad, Bihar and Ors.
rules.relevance: Held that if a person is in custody with no imminent possibility of release, the power of preventive detention should not be exercised; cogent materials for potential release must be apparent.

rules.case_name: Ramesh Yadav vs District Magistrate, Etah and Ors.
rules.reference: Ramesh Yadav vs District Magistrate, Etah and Ors.
rules.relevance: Held that an order of detention should not ordinarily be passed merely on the ground that an under-trial prisoner is likely to get bail without opposing bail or challenging its grant.

rules.case_name: Masood Alam v. Union of India
rules.reference: Masood Alam v. Union of India
rules.relevance: Held that detention of a person in jail is valid only if there is relevant material showing the person is likely to be released soon and will then indulge in prejudicial activities.

rules.case_name: Ramesh Yadav vs District Magistrate, Etah & Ors.
rules.reference: Ramesh Yadav vs District Magistrate, Etah & Ors.
rules.relevance: Cited for the view that detention should not ordinarily be passed merely on the likelihood of bail. Distinguished by the court based on the specific facts and cogent material in the present case.

rules.case_name: Merugu Satyanarayana v. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.reference: Merugu Satyanarayana v. State of Andhra Pradesh
rules.relevance: Held that the detaining authority must subjectively satisfy itself that detention is necessary despite the person already being in jail, and a subordinate police officer cannot arrogate this satisfaction.

rules.reference: Authenticity of Notice
rules.relevance: Knowledge of a court order must be obtained from an authorized or authentic source; an unverified telegram or unsigned application without an affidavit does not constitute valid notice.

rules.reference: Parties to Contempt Appeals
rules.relevance: The court held that judges deciding a contempt matter have no personal interest in the result and no relief is claimed against them; thus, they need not be made parties to the appeal.

rules.reference: Intentional Disobedience for Contempt
rules.relevance: For a subordinate court to be guilty of contempt for disobeying a superior court's order, the disobedience must be intentional, which requires knowledge of the order.

rules.case_name: Ambard vs Attorney General for Trinidad & Tobago
rules.reference: Ambard vs Attorney General for Trinidad & Tobago
rules.relevance: Cited to illustrate the practice in other jurisdictions where the Attorney General, rather than judges, is made a party in contempt appeals.

rules.case_name: Tukaram Gaokar vs S.N. Shukla
rules.reference: Good Faith Inquiry
rules.relevance: Relied on for the principle that an authority holding an inquiry in good faith is not guilty of contempt merely because parallel proceedings are pending before a court.

rules.reference: Cinematograph Act, 1918
rules.relevance: This section empowers the State Government to make rules for carrying into effect the provisions of the Act, which was the basis for the impugned notifications.

rules.reference: U.P. Cinema (Regulation) Act, 1955
rules.relevance: Establishes the requirement for a licence to exhibit films and constitutes the District Magistrate as the Licensing Authority.

rules.reference: U.P. Cinematograph Rules, 1951
rules.relevance: Prohibits licensing if the building is within 75 meters of a recognized educational institution; the determination of such status is final at the certificate stage.

rules.reference: U.P. Cinematograph Rules, 1951
rules.relevance: Governs the application for and grant of a certificate of approval for the site and plans of a cinema building.

rules.reference: Public Interest Parameters
rules.relevance: The parameters of public interest at the stage of site approval differ from those at the stage of licence grant; prior determinations on specific rules cannot be revisited under the guise of public interest.

rules.reference: Representation of the People Act, 1951
rules.relevance: Provides that a person is not qualified to be chosen to fill a seat reserved for Scheduled Tribes unless they are a member of a Scheduled Tribe.

rules.case_name: Dilworth vs Commissioner of Stamps
rules.reference: Statutory Interpretation of 'Including'
rules.relevance: Cited to explain that the word 'including' can be used to extend meaning or as a synonym for 'means' depending on context, rejecting the argument that its omission necessarily broadens the scope.

rules.reference: Structure of Scheduled Tribes Schedule
rules.relevance: Communities listed under a specific entry are presumed to have mutual affinity with the main tribe named in that entry, consistent with Article 342's reference to 'parts of or groups within' tribes.

rules.reference: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Order (Amendment) Act, 1976
rules.relevance: Amended the Schedule to the Order; the appellant relied on the structural changes in this amendment to argue for a broader interpretation of 'Mana'.

rules.case_name: Dina vs Narayan Singh
rules.reference: Dina vs Narayan Singh
rules.relevance: Established that the appellant belongs to the 'Kshatriya Bidwaik Mana' community and that the 'Mana' entry in the previous schedule referred only to the sub-tribe with affinity to Gonds.

rules.case_name: Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj vs State of Rajasthan & Ors.
rules.reference: Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj vs State of Rajasthan & Ors.
rules.relevance: Held that participation of the public in Darshan and festivals is a strong factor in determining the public character of a temple.

rules.case_name: Goswami Shri Mahalaxmi Vahuji vs Rannchhoddas Kalidas & Ors.
rules.reference: Goswami Shri Mahalaxmi Vahuji vs Rannchhoddas Kalidas & Ors.
rules.relevance: Established factors to determine if a temple is public or private, including origin, management, gifts, and rights of devotees.

rules.case_name: Pujari Lakshmana Goundan vs Subramania Ayyar
rules.reference: Pujari Lakshmana Goundan vs Subramania Ayyar
rules.relevance: Held that if a founder holds out a temple as public, it can be inferred that the temple was dedicated to the public.

rules.reference: Management does not imply ownership
rules.relevance: The fact that management of a temple remains with a ruler or family does not necessarily indicate that the temple is private property.

rules.reference: Inference of dedication from long user
rules.relevance: In the absence of a written grant, long and uninterrupted user by the public is a material factor from which an inference of dedication may arise.

rules.reference: Insufficiency of Formal Apology
rules.relevance: The court reasoned that accepting a belated, formal apology made only under compulsion would amount to issuing a license to scandalize courts with impunity, as it imposes negligible cost on the contemnor.

rules.reference: Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
rules.relevance: Defines criminal contempt as any act which scandalizes or tends to scandalize, or lowers or tends to lower the authority of, any Court.

rules.reference: Exercise of Contempt Jurisdiction
rules.relevance: While contempt jurisdiction must be exercised sparingly and with circumspection, it must be enforced to maintain the morale of judges and the decorum of the court, avoiding unmerited leniency at the cost of principle.

rules.reference: Maintenance of Judicial Independence
rules.relevance: The court held that judicial independence requires protection from intimidation and character assassination by disgruntled advocates, ensuring judges can decide matters according to conscience without fear.

rules.reference: Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
rules.relevance: The provision allowing for the remission of punishment upon tendering an apology, which the High Court applied.

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: Bars appeal against a decree passed in terms of a compromise agreement (consent decree).

rules.case_name: Tarini Charan Bhattacharjee vs Kedar Nath Haldar
rules.reference: Tarini Charan Bhattacharjee vs Kedar Nath Haldar
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that questions of jurisdiction and pure questions of law unrelated to the rights of parties are not res judicata.

rules.reference: Res judicata does not apply to erroneous decisions on jurisdiction
rules.relevance: The court held that a rule of procedure cannot supersede the law of the land; therefore, an erroneous decision on jurisdiction cannot operate as res judicata.

rules.reference: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
rules.relevance: Permits partial compromise and mandates the court to record it and pass a decree in terms of the agreement.

rules.reference: Res judicata applies to consent decrees
rules.relevance: The court held that a consent decree, if not vitiated by fraud, misrepresentation, mistake, or misunderstanding, is as binding upon the parties as a decree passed by invitum and bars subsequent suits on the same matter.

rules.reference: Andhra Pradesh (Telengana Area) District Municipalities Act, 1956
rules.relevance: The court examined this section to determine if the absence of specific designations in the master plan invalidated the applicability of the Central Act to Warangal.

rules.reference: Plenary power of Parliament under Article 252(1)
rules.relevance: The court held that once Parliament is invested with power under Article 252(1), it has plenary power to structure the Act, including specifying states and categories in the Schedule, to facilitate adoption by other states.

rules.case_name: Jatin Chakravorty vs Sri Justice H. K. Bose
rules.reference: Jatin Chakravorty vs Sri Justice H. K. Bose
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to support the view that the Governor does not vote on resolutions and thus is not part of the 'Legislature' for the purpose of passing resolutions under Article 252(1).

rules.reference: Andhra Pradesh State and Subordinate Services Rules
rules.relevance: Rule 47 empowers the Governor to deal with cases of appointment in a manner just and equitable, without being limited by general rules made under Article 309 or continued under Article 313 of the Constitution.

rules.reference: Entry 18, List II of the Seventh Schedule
rules.relevance: The court identified this entry as the subject matter ('Land') over which State Legislatures have exclusive power, which was transferred to Parliament via Article 252.

rules.case_name: Pandurang Tukia and Bhillia vs The State of Hyderabad
rules.reference: Pandurang Tukia and Bhillia vs The State of Hyderabad
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case to hold that the principle of not imposing the death penalty when appellate judges differ applies only when they differ on the question of sentence, not when they differ on guilt.

rules.case_name: Nar Singh and Anr. vs The State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.reference: Nar Singh and Anr. vs The State of Uttar Pradesh
rules.relevance: The court referred to this case to explain that a certificate is proper only if there is an error of a fundamental character, such as a misreading of evidence leading to a wrongful conviction.

rules.reference: Criminal Procedure Code
rules.relevance: The court interpreted this section to determine that when judges are equally divided, the third judge's opinion forms the basis of the judgment without a mandatory requirement to specifically refute the acquitting judge's opinion as in appeals against acquittal.

rules.reference: Criminal Procedure Code
rules.relevance: The court held that adverse inferences could not be drawn from the accused's silence regarding specific facts (such as blood on the chabutra or absconding) because these facts were not put to them during examination under this section.

rules.case_name: Pritam Singh vs State
rules.reference: Pritam Singh vs State
rules.relevance: Cited for the rule that appellate courts should interfere if there is a miscarriage of justice due to the failure to consider important circumstances or the erroneous placement of the burden of proof.

rules.reference: Criminal Procedure Code
rules.relevance: This section requires the sanction of the appropriate Government for the prosecution of public servants for acts done in the discharge of official duties.

rules.reference: Criminal Procedure Code
rules.relevance: This section authorizes the Provincial Government to confer powers of a Magistrate on any person for the trial of particular cases.

rules.case_name: Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King
rules.reference: Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to establish that lacunas in a sanction order can be remedied by specific evidence during the trial.

rules.case_name: Anwar Ali Sarkar v. Emperor
rules.reference: Anwar Ali Sarkar v. Emperor
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case, noting it applies only where the special procedure is materially different from and prejudicial to the accused compared to normal procedure.

rules.reference: Criminal Procedure Code
rules.relevance: This section grants the sanctioning Government the discretionary power to specify the Court before which the trial is to be held.

rules.reference: Father's Power to Partition
rules.relevance: A Hindu father has the power to partition joint family property and disrupt joint status without the consent of his sons.

rules.reference: Ineffectiveness of Will for Ancestral Property
rules.relevance: A father has no power to dispose of ancestral joint family property by will; such a will is ineffective.

rules.case_name: Bhagwan Dayal vs Smt. Reoti Devi
rules.reference: No Presumption of Continued Unity
rules.relevance: There is no presumption that remaining coparceners remain united after one member separates; it is a question of fact whether they agreed to remain united.

rules.case_name: M. N. Aryamurthy & Anr. vs M. D. Subbaraya Setty
rules.reference: Requirements for Family Arrangement
rules.relevance: A family arrangement requires an agreement among members to compromise disputed rights and must be intended to operate from the date of execution.

rules.reference: Coparcenary as a Creature of Law
rules.relevance: A coparcenary cannot be created by agreement among members (except in reunion) and 'branch-wise' partition is unknown to Hindu law.

rules.reference: Companies Act, 1913
rules.relevance: Imposes penalty for default in complying with Section 131 (laying balance sheet before general meeting). The court held that failure to call the meeting is not a defense if directors were responsible.

rules.reference: A person charged with an offence cannot rely on his own default as an answer to the charge
rules.relevance: The core principle adopted by the court to rule that directors cannot escape liability for filing defaults by claiming the prerequisite general meeting was not called, if they were responsible for not calling it.

rules.reference: Companies Act, 1913
rules.relevance: Imposes penalty on officers who knowingly and wilfully authorise default in filing the summary of share capital. The court interpreted this to mean liability arises even if the meeting was not held, provided the officer was responsible for the failure to call it.

rules.case_name: Park vs Lawton
rules.reference: Park vs Lawton
rules.relevance: English precedent supporting the view that an officer cannot defeat statutory provisions by wilfully failing to call a general meeting.

rules.case_name: Imperator vs The Pioneer Clay and Industrial Works Ltd.
rules.reference: Imperator vs The Pioneer Clay and Industrial Works Ltd.
rules.relevance: The case relied upon by lower courts was distinguished because it concerned Section 134, which had different language, and the Supreme Court suggested it may not have been correctly decided regarding the principle of self-induced default.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Income Tax, Punjab & N.W.F.P. vs Nawal Kishore Kharaiti Lai
rules.reference: Commissioner of Income Tax, Punjab & N.W.F.P. vs Nawal Kishore Kharaiti Lai
rules.relevance: Applied by analogy to hold that a prior order declaring a person as a principal officer is not obligatory before assessment proceedings commence.

rules.reference: Indian Income Tax Act, 1922
rules.relevance: Defined 'principal officer' and the procedure for serving notices, allowing the Income Tax Officer to serve notice on a person intended to be treated as the principal officer.

rules.reference: Res Judicata in Income Tax
rules.relevance: A decision on a question of fact or law in one assessment year is not binding in another year; findings are conclusive only for the year of assessment.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Income Tax, U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndicate
rules.reference: Commissioner of Income Tax, U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndicate
rules.relevance: Demonstrated that the Appellate Tribunal has the power to set aside assessments, indicating that the Income Tax Officer's discretion is subject to judicial review and not arbitrary.

rules.case_name: Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay vs Laxmidas
rules.reference: Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay vs Laxmidas
rules.relevance: Held that the fact that one individual is a minor does not affect the existence of an association of persons if they associated for the purpose of gain.

rules.reference: Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948
rules.relevance: The court considered these provisions to determine that sickness benefits under the Act do not substitute for the right to sick leave with full pay.

rules.case_name: Crown Aluminium Works Ltd. v. Their Workmen
rules.reference: Crown Aluminium Works Ltd. v. Their Workmen
rules.relevance: The court referred to this case to emphasize the need to consider the problem of wage fixation on an industry cum region basis and the ability of the industry to pay.

rules.case_name: French Motor Car Co. Ltd. v. Its Workmen
rules.reference: French Motor Car Co. Ltd. v. Its Workmen
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to support the Tribunal's discretion in deciding the adjustment of existing employees into new wage scales based on the circumstances of the case.

rules.case_name: Alembic Chemical Works Company Ltd. vs Its Workmen
rules.reference: Alembic Chemical Works Company Ltd. vs Its Workmen
rules.relevance: Supports the beneficent construction that an adjudicator can grant terms more liberal than those provided by statute, interpreting 'any award' to include future awards.

rules.case_name: Express Newspapers Ltd. v. Their Workmen
rules.reference: Express Newspapers Ltd. v. Their Workmen
rules.relevance: The court referred to this case to support the principle of considering the ability of the industry to pay when fixing wages.

rules.reference: PEC Employees' (Conduct, Discipline & Appeal) Rules, 1975
rules.relevance: Requires the Appellate Authority to consider findings and penalty adequacy. The court found this rule was violated due to lack of reasoned order.

rules.case_name: Sukhdev Singh vs Bhagatram Sardar Singh Raghuvanshi
rules.reference: Sukhdev Singh vs Bhagatram Sardar Singh Raghuvanshi
rules.relevance: Established that employment under State instrumentalities is public employment and a declaration of continuance in service can be granted if termination is illegal.

rules.reference: PEC Employees' (Conduct, Discipline & Appeal) Rules, 1975
rules.relevance: Obligates the Inquiry Officer to provide findings and reasons. The court found this rule was violated.

rules.reference: PEC Employees' (Conduct, Discipline & Appeal) Rules, 1975
rules.relevance: Rule 4 sets general norms of behavior, while Rule 5 enumerates specific misconduct. The court held that violation of general norms does not constitute misconduct unless specified in Rule 5.

rules.case_name: M/s Glaxo Laboratories (I) Ltd vs Presiding Officer, Labour Court
rules.reference: M/s Glaxo Laboratories (I) Ltd vs Presiding Officer, Labour Court
rules.relevance: Held that misconduct must be prescribed with precision and cannot be left to ex post facto interpretation by management.

rules.reference: Working Journalists Industrial Disputes Act, 1955
rules.relevance: Defines 'working journalist' as a person whose principal avocation is that of a journalist and who is employed as such in a newspaper establishment. The court interpreted the conditions of principal avocation and employment.

rules.reference: Requirement of Exclusive Employment
rules.relevance: The court reasoned that the benefits under the Act (e.g., retrenchment, gratuity) imply a master-servant relationship, which necessitates exclusive employment by the newspaper establishment.

rules.reference: Statutory Interpretation of 'Includes' Clause
rules.relevance: The court held that the 'includes' clause listing specific roles like 'correspondent' serves to clarify that these roles are journalistic, but does not dispense with the primary conditions of principal avocation and employment.

rules.reference: Interpretation of 'Principal Avocation'
rules.relevance: The court determined that 'avocation' in this context means vocation or profession. The decisive test for 'principal avocation' is the comparison of gains (income) from journalism versus other professions, not merely the time spent.

rules.reference: Status of Part-Time Employees
rules.relevance: The court held that part-time employment is not excluded from the definition of a working journalist, provided the statutory tests of principal avocation and employment are satisfied.

rules.reference: Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913
rules.relevance: The court interpreted the statutory hierarchy of pre-emption rights, specifically the definition of 'other co-sharers' in clause 'Fourthly' relative to clauses 'First', 'Secondly', and 'Thirdly'.

rules.case_name: Atam Prakash vs State of Haryana and Others
rules.reference: Atam Prakash vs State of Haryana and Others
rules.relevance: This decision declared clauses 'First', 'Secondly', and 'Thirdly' of Section 15(1)(a) and (b) ultra vires, which formed the basis for the High Court's dismissal and the context for the petitioners' alternative claim.

rules.case_name: Atam Parkash vs State of Haryana
rules.reference: Atam Parkash vs State of Haryana
rules.relevance: The court relied on this Constitution Bench decision which declared clauses 'First', 'Secondly', and 'Thirdly' in Section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913 ultra vires the Constitution due to lack of reasonable classification.

rules.case_name: Amir Singh & Anr. vs Ram Singh & Ors.
rules.reference: Amir Singh & Anr. vs Ram Singh & Ors.
rules.relevance: The court relied on this Constitution Bench decision to establish that the retrospective operation of Section 31 makes the substantive provisions of Section 15 retrospective, deeming the right to vest at the relevant time.

rules.reference: Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913 (as amended)
rules.relevance: The court held that due to the retrospective operation of the 1960 Amendment, this clause granting pre-emption rights to tenants was deemed to exist at the time of the sale.

rules.provision: Paragraph 292 of the Sastry Award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal
rules.reference: Interpretation of Award Provisions
rules.relevance: The court interpreted the specific provisions for pay adjustment. The absence of a specific increment date for workmen joining after January 31, 1950, contrasted with the explicit April 1 date for earlier employees, implied that increments for the former group follow the anniversary of their appointment.

rules.reference: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
rules.relevance: The statutory basis for the appellant's application to the Labour Court regarding changes in conditions of service.

rules.reference: Standard for Review of Judgment
rules.relevance: A review petition requires the petitioner to demonstrate an error apparent on the face of the record. The court found the Bank failed to satisfy this burden regarding the basis of appointment.

rules.case_name: Standard Vacuum Refining Co. of India Ltd. v. Its Workmen
rules.reference: Standard Vacuum Refining Co. of India Ltd. v. Its Workmen
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case for the principles of wage fixation, including the concepts of minimum basic wage, fair wage, and living wage, and the need to consider social conscience and national economy.

rules.case_name: French Motor Car Co. Ltd. v. Its Workmen
rules.reference: French Motor Car Co. Ltd. v. Its Workmen
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to support the Tribunal's discretion in deciding the adjustment of existing employees into new wage scales based on the circumstances of the case.

rules.reference: Natural conduct of witnesses
rules.relevance: The court evaluated the credibility of the witness based on whether her conduct (silence and delay in identification) was natural and probable under the circumstances.

rules.reference: Appellate court's jurisdiction in reversing acquittal
rules.relevance: The court held that while appellate jurisdiction is coextensive with the trial court, it should be slow to interfere if two views are reasonably possible and reasons for reversal must be cogent.

rules.reference: Presumption of Intention
rules.relevance: The court held that when an injury is inflicted, there is a presumption that the accused intended to inflict that particular injury, which can only be rebutted by evidence showing the act was accidental or unintentional.

rules.reference: Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction Act, 1970
rules.relevance: The statutory provision under which the criminal appeal was filed before the Supreme Court.

rules.reference: Criminal Procedure Code
rules.relevance: The court analyzed the delay and inconsistencies in the recording of the first information report under this section.

rules.reference: Evacuee Property Act
rules.relevance: This section empowers the Central Government to make rules providing for circumstances in which leases and allotments may be cancelled, validating the restrictive nature of Rule 14(6).

rules.reference: Administration of Evacuee Property Rules, 1950
rules.relevance: This rule, as amended on July 22, 1952, restricts the cancellation of quasi-permanent allotments of rural evacuee property to specific grounds enumerated in the rule.

rules.reference: Evacuee Property Act
rules.relevance: This section confers wide powers on the Custodian, but the court held these powers are subject to the rules made under the Act.

rules.reference: Evacuee Property Act
rules.relevance: This section confers revisional powers on the Custodian General, but the court interpreted these powers as limited to correcting errors within the scope of what the subordinate authority was permitted to do.

rules.reference: Superior authority cannot exercise powers denied to subordinate authority
rules.relevance: The court ruled that the Custodian General cannot do something which the Custodian or District Judge could not have done or was prohibited from doing.

rules.reference: Public interest in licensing terms
rules.relevance: The court invoked the principle of public interest to direct a revision of the license fee and terms, ensuring they were not detrimental to the public despite the statutory validity of the grant.

rules.reference: The West Bengal Estates Acquisition Rules, 1954
rules.relevance: This rule requires the Collector to grant a summary settlement specifying terms and conditions. The court found the Collector failed to perform this statutory duty.

rules.reference: The West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953
rules.relevance: This section mandates the Revenue Officer to determine the rent payable for land retained by intermediaries. The court considered this to establish that lease execution and rent payment are contingent upon this determination.

rules.reference: Intrinsic character of a public park
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that development work is permissible provided it does not destroy the intrinsic character of the park as a place of public recreation.

rules.case_name: Attorney General vs Corporation of Sunderland
rules.reference: Attorney General vs Corporation of Sunderland
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case to reject the argument that the Corporation acts as a trustee and cannot use park land for purposes other than those strictly contemplated, noting the intrinsic character of the park was preserved.

rules.case_name: State of U.P. vs Deoman Upadhyaya
rules.reference: State of U.P. vs Deoman Upadhyaya
rules.relevance: Distinguished on the basis that the conviction in that case relied on a complete chain of circumstances, not merely the production of a blood-stained weapon.

rules.reference: Circumstantial Evidence
rules.relevance: Circumstantial evidence must form a complete chain consistent only with the guilt of the accused and inconsistent with innocence.

rules.case_name: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Singhara Singh and Others
rules.reference: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Singhara Singh and Others
rules.relevance: Held that a confession recorded by a Second Class Magistrate not specially empowered during an investigation is inadmissible, and oral evidence of such confession is also barred.

rules.case_name: Pulukuri Kotayya vs King Emperor
rules.reference: Pulukuri Kotayya vs King Emperor
rules.relevance: Established that 'fact discovered' under Section 27 refers to the place of concealment and the accused's knowledge of it, not the past history or use of the object.

rules.reference: Indian Evidence Act, 1872
rules.relevance: Statements made to a police officer without the voluntary intervention of a Magistrate are inadmissible.

rules.reference: Identity of Assessable Unit
rules.relevance: The court established that the true question is the identity of the unit assessed under the Income-tax Act. A firm retains its identity as an assessable unit despite changes in partners, provided there is no dissolution or division of assets.

rules.reference: Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
rules.relevance: These provisions support the position that the technical view of partnership under general law (where a firm has no legal existence apart from partners) cannot be strictly applied to income tax assessment.

rules.reference: Interpretation of Partnership Deeds
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that when a deed recites a transaction is effective from a particular date, the context determines whether the date is included or excluded. This helped interpret the dissolution and formation dates in the partnership instrument.

rules.reference: Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1939 (VII of 1939)
rules.relevance: This Act inserted Section 25(4) into the Income Tax Act and came into force on April 1, 1939. It defines the critical temporal point for determining eligibility for relief.

rules.reference: General Clauses Act, 1897
rules.relevance: This provision establishes that a Central Act comes into operation immediately on the expiration of the day preceding its commencement. It was used to determine that the 1939 Amendment Act came into force immediately after midnight on March 31, 1939.

rules.case_name: Hamzeh Malas and Sons vs British Imex Industries Ltd.
rules.reference: Hamzeh Malas and Sons vs British Imex Industries Ltd.
rules.relevance: Held that a confirmed letter of credit imposes an absolute obligation on the banker to pay irrespective of disputes between the parties as to whether the goods are up to contract.

rules.reference: Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits (1962 Revision), International Chamber of Commerce Brochure No. 222
rules.relevance: Establishes that in documentary credit operations, parties deal in documents and not in goods, and payment against compliant documents binds the authorizing party.

rules.reference: Pleading Requirements
rules.relevance: Contentions regarding the modification of a contract based on the intention of parties must be pleaded and cannot be raised for the first time in appeal.

rules.reference: Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits (1962 Revision), International Chamber of Commerce Brochure No. 222
rules.relevance: Establishes that an irrevocable credit is a definite undertaking by the issuing bank to pay, which cannot be modified or cancelled without the agreement of all concerned.

rules.reference: Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits (1962 Revision), International Chamber of Commerce Brochure No. 222
rules.relevance: Establishes that banks assume no liability for the description, quantity, quality, condition, or existence of the goods represented by the documents.

rules.case_name: Om Prakash Gupta vs Dig Vijendrapal Gupta
rules.reference: Om Prakash Gupta vs Dig Vijendrapal Gupta
rules.relevance: Distinguished because in that case the building had not yet become ten years old when the revision was decided, whereas in the present case it did.

rules.case_name: Om Prakash Gupta vs Dig Vijendrapal Gupta
rules.reference: Om Prakash Gupta vs Dig Vijendrapal Gupta
rules.relevance: Established that Section 39 applies only if the suit was pending on the date of commencement of the Act (15th July 1972) and that the exemption under Section 2(2) applies to buildings constructed before the Act.

rules.reference: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: The court held that this section, providing benefits during pendency, was inapplicable because the Act itself did not apply to the building due to the Section 2(2) exemption.

rules.reference: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: The court interpreted this provision to determine that the Act exempts buildings for ten years from completion, and that for assessed buildings, the date of first assessment is the deemed date of completion.

rules.case_name: Ram Saroop Rai vs Lilavati
rules.reference: Ram Saroop Rai vs Lilavati
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to support the view that the Act applies based on the explicit language of Section 2(2), distinguishing it from earlier conflicting authority.

rules.case_name: Baldev Krishna Sahi vs Shipping Corpn. of India Ltd.
rules.reference: Baldev Krishna Sahi vs Shipping Corpn. of India Ltd.
rules.relevance: Established that Section 630 applies to past officers or employees who wrongfully withhold company property after the termination of their employment.

rules.reference: Companies Act, 1956
rules.relevance: Provides for penalty and recovery of property wrongfully obtained or withheld by an officer or employee of a company. The court interpreted this to include former employees who withhold property after termination.

rules.reference: Bona fide dispute test
rules.relevance: A dispute is not 'bona fide' if it is fabricated by an employee through self-serving documents or if the employee's claim contradicts their own prior admissions and the primary agreement.

rules.reference: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898
rules.relevance: Considered to determine if any irregularity in the filing of the complaint was curable.

rules.case_name: Damodar Das Jain vs Krishna Charan Chakraborti
rules.reference: Damodar Das Jain vs Krishna Charan Chakraborti
rules.relevance: Held that criminal courts should not adjudicate if there is a bona fide dispute regarding title. The Supreme Court distinguished this case on facts, finding no bona fide dispute here.

rules.reference: Resolution of Government (Home Department No. 3264 (Rev))
rules.relevance: Authorized the redemption of existing land revenue by immediate payment of a sum equal in value to the revenue redeemed, confirming the government's intent to extinguish the recurring demand.

rules.reference: The Land Law of Bengal (Tagore Law Lectures, 1895)
rules.relevance: Cited to support the classification of lands granted proprietary title free from land revenue in consideration of a capitalized sum as 'revenue free' lands.

rules.case_name: Kamakshya Narain Singh vs Commissioner of Income Tax
rules.reference: Kamakshya Narain Singh vs Commissioner of Income Tax
rules.relevance: The Patna High Court decision initially binding on the department, which was later reversed by the Privy Council, forming the factual basis for the reassessment.

rules.case_name: Madan Lal vs Commissioner of I. T., Punjab
rules.reference: Madan Lal vs Commissioner of I. T., Punjab
rules.relevance: Supports the view that Section 34 applies where income is included in a return but left unassessed or assessment is cancelled.

rules.case_name: Rajendranath Mukherjee vs Income tax Commissioner
rules.reference: Rajendranath Mukherjee vs Income tax Commissioner
rules.relevance: The appellant relied on this to argue that returned income cannot escape assessment; the court distinguished it, holding it applied only to pending proceedings, not final orders.

rules.reference: Rajasthan Laws (Application to Sirohi) Act, 1953
rules.relevance: Demonstrates that Rajasthan laws do not automatically apply to Sirohi upon merger unless specifically included in the Schedule of this Act.

rules.reference: Rajasthan Ordinance No. 16 of 1949
rules.relevance: Authorized the Government of Rajasthan to issue a revised tariff, but the court determined it did not apply to Sirohi at the relevant time.

rules.reference: Sirohi Customs Act, 1944
rules.relevance: Establishes that customs duties can only be levied on goods specifically mentioned in the Tariff at prescribed rates.

rules.reference: Sirohi Regency Act, 1947
rules.relevance: Deems the Board of Regency to be the 'Ruler' for constitutional and legal purposes during the minority.

rules.reference: Notification constituting the Council of State, Sirohi
rules.relevance: Indicates that the Council's power regarding new taxation is advisory and requires final orders from the Ruler (Board of Regency) to be effective.

rules.reference: Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972
rules.relevance: Allows the Government to exempt establishments where employees receive benefits not less favorable than those under the Act, indicating the Act does not rigidly standardize gratuity schemes.

rules.reference: Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972
rules.relevance: Provides that nothing in the section affects the right of an employee to receive better terms of gratuity under any award, agreement, or contract with the employer.

rules.reference: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
rules.relevance: Confers discretion on the Tribunal to decide the date from which an award comes into operation; appellate courts do not interfere unless the discretion is unreasonably exercised.

rules.case_name: Alembic Chemical Works Company Ltd. vs Its Workmen
rules.reference: Alembic Chemical Works Company Ltd. vs Its Workmen
rules.relevance: Supports the beneficent construction that an adjudicator can grant terms more liberal than those provided by statute, interpreting 'any award' to include future awards.

rules.reference: Uniformity in industrial awards
rules.relevance: Uniformity in awards within the same industry is highly desirable, particularly regarding dearness allowance linkage.

rules.case_name: Ludichem Agencies Etc. vs Ahmed R.V. Peer Mohamed
rules.reference: Ludichem Agencies Etc. vs Ahmed R.V. Peer Mohamed
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that a licence terminates with the tenancy of the licensor, but distinguished on facts where the licence was created before the tenancy ended.

rules.reference: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
rules.relevance: The central issue was whether a licensee of a statutory tenant, created before 1st February 1973, is deemed a tenant under this section.

rules.case_name: D.N. Banerji vs P.R. Mukharjee & Ors.
rules.reference: D.N. Banerji vs P.R. Mukharjee & Ors.
rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that High Courts should not interfere with factual findings under Articles 226/227 unless there is a grave miscarriage of justice or flagrant violation of law.

rules.case_name: Ratanlal Chandiprasad Jalan vs Raniram Darkhan
rules.citation: Writ Petition No. 76 of 1980 (Bombay High Court Full Bench)

rules.relevance: The Full Bench held that a statutory tenant without specific contractual right to sublet could not create a valid licence; the Supreme Court disagreed with this interpretation.

rules.case_name: Babhutmal Raichand Oswal vs Laxmibai R. Tarte
rules.reference: Babhutmal Raichand Oswal vs Laxmibai R. Tarte
rules.relevance: Cited to establish that the High Court cannot convert itself into a court of appeal under Article 227 to correct errors of fact.

rules.reference: Income Tax Act, 1961

rules.reference: Distinction between Purpose and Powers
rules.relevance: Distinguishes between the charitable purpose of a trust and the powers conferred on trustees (e.g., employee benefits) which are incidental to the proper functioning of the organization.

rules.case_name: Additional Commissioner of Income Tax, Gujarat vs Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers' Association
rules.reference: Additional Commissioner of Income Tax, Gujarat vs Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers' Association
rules.relevance: Established the 'doctrine of dominant or primary object', holding that if the primary object is charitable, incidental profit-making activities do not disqualify the trust from exemption.

rules.case_name: Indian Chamber of Commerce v. Commissioner of Income Tax

rules.relevance: The majority distinguished this case, disagreeing with the view that any activity for profit in advancing the object disqualifies the purpose, arguing instead that the object itself must not involve profit-making as its predominant motive.

rules.reference: Motor Vehicles Act, 1939

rules.reference: Motor Vehicles Act, 1939

rules.reference: Motor Vehicles Act, 1939
rules.relevance: The provision enabling All India Permits was analyzed to determine if it implicitly obligated states to grant tax exemptions.

rules.reference: Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948

rules.reference: Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948
rules.relevance: The court interpreted this section to determine the duty of the Manager to collect rent and interest and pay it to the landholder, implying an obligation to pay interest on withheld amounts.

rules.case_name: State of Bihar v. Gopi Kishore Prasad

rules.case_name: High Commissioner for India v. I. M. Lall

rules.reference: Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944

rules.case_name: Barendra Kumar Ghosh vs Emperor

rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that classification in services must have a rational nexus with the object sought and that equal pay for unequal work is a negation of Article 14.

rules.case_name: Bhartiya Dak Tar Mazdoor Manch vs Union of India & Ors.
rules.reference: Bhartiya Dak Tar Mazdoor Manch vs Union of India & Ors.
rules.relevance: The Court relied on this judgment to apply the same directions regarding wage parity and absorption schemes to contingent staff in the Income Tax Department, citing similar facts and circumstances.

rules.reference: Res judicata / Issue estoppel regarding findings of fact

rules.case_name: Dhirendra Chamoli and Another vs State of U.P.

rules.case_name: Padfield and Others vs Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food and Others
rules.reference: Padfield and Others vs Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food and Others
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to reject the argument that unfettered discretion precludes judicial review, emphasizing that authorities must consider complaints properly.

rules.reference: Life Insurance Corporation Act, 1956
rules.relevance: Conferred paramount power on the Central Government to alter terms and conditions of service, overriding any contrary provisions in subordinate instruments.

rules.case_name: High Court of Andhra Pradesh and ors. vs V.V.S. Krishnamurity and ors.
rules.reference: High Court of Andhra Pradesh and ors. vs V.V.S. Krishnamurity and ors.
rules.relevance: Cited to confirm that the power under Article 235 is exclusive, comprehensive, and effective, covering premature retirement.

rules.reference: Rules of Court, 1952 (Allahabad High Court)
rules.relevance: Provides that irregularities in procedure shall not affect the validity of orders. The court held that the failure to obtain a prior recommendation is an incurable defect/illegality, not a mere irregularity curable by this rule.

rules.reference: Rules of Court, 1952 (Allahabad High Court)
rules.relevance: Defines the administrative structure of the High Court. Rule 5 mandates that the Judge in the Administrative Department must consult the Administrative Committee on important matters, including those where the Government desires the Court's opinion. The Administrative Judge alone cannot act for the Court in such matters.

rules.case_name: State of Uttar Pradesh vs Batuk Deo Patil Tripathi & Anr.
rules.reference: State of Uttar Pradesh vs Batuk Deo Patil Tripathi & Anr.
rules.relevance: Established that premature retirement of subordinate judicial officers falls within the control of the High Court under Article 235 and requires its recommendation.

rules.reference: Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970
rules.relevance: This provision mandated that transferred employees retain their pre-nationalization terms of service unless altered, protecting the retirement age of 60 for pre-1969 recruits.
